set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: Why does an age-adjusted death rate differ from a crude one?
opts: Adjustment removes deaths from unrelated causes
Restricting to one cause gives the cause-specific rate rather than an age-adjusted one.
Adjustment converts the rate into a proportion
Expressing deaths as a share of all deaths gives proportionate mortality rather than an adjusted rate.
Adjustment removes the effect of the population's age structure
Correct, and the difference can be substantial: a crude United States rate of about 794 per 100,000 in 2009 corresponded to an age-adjusted figure of about 741.
Adjustment changes the multiplier used
The multiplier only scales the figure for readability; adjustment changes what the figure accounts for.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

set1.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set1.q: When is a probability sample useful?
opts: When subgroups such as age or ethnicity must be investigated
Correct, because a random sample of the whole population may not deliver enough of a small subgroup to say anything about it.
When the population is too small to sample at all
The technique addresses how to sample rather than whether a population can be sampled.
When participants must be recruited quickly and cheaply
Speed and convenience describe a convenience or grab sample.
When every individual must have an equal chance
Equal chance defines a random sample; the probability sample allows the chance to differ as long as it is known.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: Which study designs allow surveillance to support hypothesis testing for aetiology?
opts: Case-control or cohort studies
Correct, and this is where surveillance hands over to analytic epidemiology: the data identify a question that a comparative design is then built to answer.
Cross-sectional surveys only
Cross-sectional work generates hypotheses rather than testing them.
Randomised controlled trials only
Assigning an exposure suspected of causing harm is not how aetiologic questions are investigated.
Case reports and case series
Descriptive designs characterise cases without the comparison needed to test an aetiologic hypothesis.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: Why are rates used rather than raw counts?
opts: Rates are easier to collect than counts
A rate requires the count plus a denominator, so it takes more information rather than less.
Rates allow comparisons
Correct. Two places with different populations cannot be compared on counts alone, which is why a denominator and a time period are built into the measure.
Rates remove the effect of chance
Random variation affects rates as much as counts; what rates provide is comparability.
Rates establish the cause of a disease
Rates measure how much disease there is rather than what produced it.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: What does distribution by person involve?
opts: Mapping where cases occur geographically
Mapping where cases occur is distribution by place rather than by person, which profiles who was affected.
Profiling those affected, including behaviour as well as demographics
Correct, and the questions are deliberately practical: where they eat, where they shop, what products they use, their drinking water, and whether they attended the same event.
Plotting the number of cases against time
Plotting cases against time produces an epidemic curve, which is distribution by time.
Comparing rates between nations
International comparison uses measures such as the infant mortality rate rather than describing who is affected.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: Cardiovascular disease accounted for about 24.5 per cent of United States deaths in a year. Which measure is that?
opts: Cause-specific mortality rate
That would set cardiovascular deaths against the population rather than against all deaths.
Case fatality
Case fatality sets deaths against those diagnosed with the disease rather than against all deaths.
Proportionate mortality
Correct, and it is a fraction rather than a rate, since its denominator is total deaths rather than the population at risk.
Crude death rate
The crude rate covers deaths from all causes set against the population.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 11

set1.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set1.q: Who should be included in the population at risk?
opts: Only those susceptible to the disease or outcome
Correct, and the example is unambiguous: men are not included in the denominator of a study of ovarian cancer.
Everyone living in the geographic area
Including people who cannot develop the outcome inflates the denominator and understates the rate.
Only those who already have the condition
Those who already have it cannot become new cases, so they belong outside an incidence denominator too.
Everyone who consented to take part
Consent determines who can be studied rather than who is at risk of the outcome.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set1.q: What did the SchoolNuts study set out to determine?
opts: The prevalence of food allergy in children aged 10 to 14
Correct, using a parent questionnaire together with allergy testing, and finding roughly one in twenty children in Melbourne affected.
Whether a new treatment for food allergy worked
Testing a treatment would require an experimental design rather than a prevalence survey.
Whether food allergy causes school absence
Prevalence studies are poor for cause and effect; this one measured how common the condition was.
The incidence of new food allergy over ten years
Following children over time for new cases would be an incidence or cohort study.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set1.q: What are prevalence studies good and bad at?
opts: Good for establishing cause, poor for planning services
The strengths run the other way: they answer what is common, not what produced it.
Good for following disease over many years
Following a population over time to see whether a condition appears describes an incidence or cohort study.
Good for measuring the severity of a condition
Severity is measured by case fatality rather than by a prevalence survey.
Good for hypotheses and service planning, poor for cause and effect
Correct, and they are relatively inexpensive, which is part of why they are a sensible first look at what is common in a community.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: What does provider reporting of morbidity allow?
opts: Calculation of the case fatality rate
Case fatality requires deaths among diagnosed cases rather than contact tracing.
Tracking of possible contacts and exposures
Correct, which is what converts a report of one case into the beginning of an investigation rather than a single data point.
Assignment of patients to control groups
Assignment belongs to experimental designs and has no role in surveillance.
Determination of the pretest probability
Pretest probability follows from prevalence rather than from provider reporting as such.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

set1.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set1.q: What is the Framingham Heart Study an example of?
opts: A prevalence, or cross-sectional, study
It follows participants over decades rather than measuring a condition at one moment.
A randomised controlled trial
Nothing was assigned; the exposures were observed as they occurred.
A case-control study
Participants were not selected by whether they had the outcome and then examined for past exposure.
An incidence, or cohort, study
Correct. It began in 1948 with an original cohort, follows multiple generations and additional cohorts, and helped identify the cardiovascular risk factors.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: What follows the testing of hypotheses in an outbreak investigation?
opts: Establishing the case definition
The case definition is set early, before hypotheses can be framed at all.
Determining whether an epidemic exists
That is settled near the beginning rather than after hypothesis testing.
Initiating control measures
Correct, and the sequence runs on from there to solving the original source, controlling the outbreak and deciding that it is over.
Plotting the epidemic curve
The curve is built while the outbreak is being characterised, before hypotheses are tested.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: What is a rate?
opts: The total number of people with a condition
A bare count of affected people is not a rate, because it carries neither a population nor a time period to be read against.
The proportion of deaths attributable to one cause
That describes proportionate mortality, which is explicitly not a rate because its denominator is deaths rather than population.
The number of times an event occurs in a fixed time period
Correct, and the reason rates exist rather than raw counts is comparison: a count means nothing until it is set against a population and a period.
The severity of a disease in those who have it
Severity is measured by case fatality rather than being what a rate means in general.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: Why is mortality listed as a surveillance strategy?
opts: Mortality rates are the most accurate measure of disease
Accuracy is not the argument; the point is that death is sometimes the first moment a case becomes visible.
Mortality determines the case definition
The case definition is established during the investigation rather than derived from deaths.
Deaths are easier to count than cases
Ease of counting is not the reason given; detection of otherwise unrecognised cases is.
Some cases are detected only at death
Correct, which makes death certification a genuine source of case finding rather than merely a record of outcome.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: Which example is given for documenting geographic distribution and spread?
opts: Vibrio infections after hurricane floods
That example is given for detecting outbreaks rather than for documenting geographic spread.
Emerging antibiotic resistance in an organism
That example illustrates monitoring changes in an infectious agent.
A person with tuberculosis on an international flight
Correct, because the exposure travels with the person, which makes the geographic question the operative one.
Influenza in a nursing home resident
That illustrates screening high-risk persons or groups as a surveillance strategy.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: What is the denominator of the maternal mortality rate?
opts: The mid-interval population of women
Population denominators belong to the crude and cause-specific death rates rather than to maternal mortality.
Total deaths from all causes
A denominator of total deaths describes proportionate mortality rather than a rate.
The number of pregnancies in the interval
The denominator used is live births rather than pregnancies.
Live births in the same interval
Correct, multiplied by 100,000, with deaths assigned to pregnancy-related causes in the numerator.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: Which rates are named as specific to maternal and child health?
opts: Crude and age-specific death rates
Those are general mortality rates applied to a whole population.
Incidence and prevalence rates
Incidence and prevalence are morbidity measures applying to any condition rather than maternal and child health rates.
Live birth rates and fetal, infant and maternal death rates
Correct, with neonatal and perinatal death rates alongside them, all of which take live births rather than population as their denominator.
Case fatality and death-to-case ratio
Those measure the lethality of a disease rather than maternal and child health.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: Which rates are grouped under morbidity rates?
opts: Crude and cause-specific death rates
Those belong to the mortality group rather than the morbidity group.
Incidence and prevalence rates
Correct. Morbidity concerns illness in the living, whereas the mortality group covers crude, age-specific, cause-specific, adjusted and case fatality rates.
Live birth and fetal death rates
Those fall under the additional rates specific to maternal and child health.
Case fatality and years of potential life lost
Those concern death among the affected rather than the frequency of illness.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

set1.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set1.q: What is another name for a prevalence study?
opts: A cohort study
Following a population over time to see whether a condition appears describes an incidence study, also called a cohort study.
A case-control study
A case-control study groups by outcome and looks back at exposure rather than measuring how common a condition is.
A cross-sectional study
Correct, because the population is assessed for the presence of a condition at one point rather than followed for its appearance.
A randomised trial
Nothing is assigned in a prevalence study; the condition is measured as found.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set1.q: Why is the age-adjusted death rate the right measure for comparing a county with its state?
opts: It counts only deaths among residents
Residency affects who is counted rather than whether the comparison is fair between different age structures.
It uses live births as the denominator
Live births are the denominator of the infant and maternal mortality rates rather than of adjusted death rates.
It expresses each cause as a percentage of deaths
That describes proportionate mortality rather than an age-adjusted rate.
It removes differences in age structure between the two
Correct, and without it a county with an older population would appear less healthy on the crude rate for that reason alone.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: Why must an investigation confirm that an epidemic truly exists?
opts: Epidemics are always reported by clinicians first
How a rise first comes to attention does not settle whether the rise is real rather than an artefact of detection.
An apparent rise may reflect detection rather than occurrence
Correct, which is why a baseline and a settled case definition come first: both awareness and definition change how many cases are found.
Endemic disease cannot produce clusters of cases
Endemic disease can produce apparent clusters, which is part of why confirmation is needed.
Attack rates cannot be determined otherwise
The attack rate is determined as part of the same investigation rather than depending on the confirmation.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: What must be determined at the start of an outbreak investigation?
opts: Whether the situation is epidemic or endemic
Correct, alongside determining the attack rate, establishing the diagnosis and the case definition, confirming that an epidemic truly exists, and characterising it by time, place and person.
Which control measures to implement
Control measures are initiated after hypotheses about source and spread have been developed and tested.
Which journal will publish the findings
Publication of the findings is not one of the steps named for investigating an outbreak.
The cost of the response
Cost is not among the steps named for investigating an outbreak.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: Why is proportionate mortality not a rate?
opts: It is measured over too short a period
The period is not the problem; the denominator is, because it counts deaths instead of people at risk.
Its denominator is deaths rather than population
Correct, and because every cause is expressed as a percentage of all deaths, the causes must sum to one hundred per cent.
It applies only to a single age group
Restriction to an age group describes the age-specific mortality rate, which is still a rate.
It cannot be compared between populations
Comparability is not what disqualifies it; the composition of its denominator is.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

set1.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set1.q: Why does surveillance need to establish a baseline?
opts: Because a baseline proves the cause of the disease
Hypothesis testing for aetiology is a separate function, carried out with case-control or cohort studies.
Because surveillance is required to be passive
Surveillance may be active or passive, and the baseline requirement applies either way.
Because baselines determine the case definition
The case definition is established during an outbreak investigation rather than derived from a baseline.
Without it a rise in cases cannot be recognised
Correct, and establishing that baseline is listed among its core purposes, alongside determining the magnitude of a health problem.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

set1.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set1.q: What must the causes in a proportionate mortality analysis sum to?
opts: One hundred per cent
Correct, because each cause is expressed as a share of all deaths in the population over the period, so together they account for every death.
The crude death rate
The crude death rate is a separate measure with population in its denominator rather than a total the shares add up to.
The number of live births
Live births are the denominator of the maternal and infant mortality rates rather than a total for cause shares.
Whatever the case fatality implies
Case fatality concerns deaths among those diagnosed with one disease rather than the distribution of all deaths.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

set1.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set1.q: Why does the case definition matter so much to measured frequency?
opts: Most clinical information lies on a continuum, not in two boxes
Correct, so where the line is drawn between case and non-case has a marked effect on how much disease the measurement finds.
Case definitions are fixed by national agencies
Definitions are established during an investigation rather than being immutable, which is why their effect on frequency matters.
Frequency depends only on the size of the population
The denominator matters, but so does what counts as a case in the numerator.
Clinical information is almost always binary
The opposite is stated: most clinical information is not binary and exists on a low-to-high continuum.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set1.q: Which method is described as useful for collecting prevalence information?
opts: Long-term follow-up of a cohort
Following a group over time measures incidence rather than prevalence.
Surveys
Correct, because a survey counts who does and does not have the condition at one time, which is exactly what prevalence requires.
Randomised assignment to an intervention
Nothing is assigned when measuring how common a condition is.
Pooling data from published trials
Pooling data from published trials describes a meta-analysis, which uses existing results rather than collecting new ones.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set1.q: What does incidence describe?
opts: Everyone who has the condition at one moment
That is prevalence, which counts existing cases as well as new ones.
The proportion of cases that prove fatal
That is case fatality, a measure of severity rather than of new occurrence.
The distribution of a condition by person and place
Distribution describes where and in whom disease occurs rather than how fast new cases appear.
New cases arising in previously healthy people
Correct, over a specified time period. That restriction to the previously healthy is what separates it from prevalence, which counts everyone who has the condition.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set1.q: What is a grab sample?
opts: Researchers take whoever they can find
Correct, and it sits alongside the convenience sample among the non-random approaches, where who ends up in the study is decided by availability.
A sample in which everyone has an equal chance
That is a random sample, in which selection probability is not merely known but identical for everyone.
A sample in which everyone has a known chance
That is a probability sample, where the chance of selection is known but need not be the same for everyone.
A sample drawn separately from each subgroup
Deliberate sampling within subgroups describes the use of a probability sample.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set1.q: What defines a random sample?
opts: Every individual has a known chance of selection
A known but possibly unequal chance defines a probability sample.
Every individual has an equal chance of selection
Correct, which is what separates it from a probability sample, where the chance of selection is known but need not be equal.
Participants are whoever is convenient to obtain
That describes a convenience sample, which is non-random and chosen because it is straightforward to obtain.
Researchers take whoever they can find
That describes a grab sample, the least structured of the approaches named.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: What example is given for monitoring changes in an infectious agent?
opts: A restaurant worker with hepatitis A
That is an example of screening high-risk persons or groups.
Foodborne gastrointestinal disease
Vibrio infections after hurricane floods are given as an example of detecting outbreaks rather than geographic spread.
Resistance emerging to an antibiotic it was once susceptible to
Correct, and it matters because the organism has not changed its name while the treatment that works against it has changed entirely.
A person with tuberculosis flying internationally
That illustrates documenting geographic distribution and spread.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: How does prevalence help in clinical reasoning?
opts: It establishes the cause of the condition
Prevalence measures how much of a condition is present rather than what produces it.
It determines the severity of the condition
Severity is measured by case fatality rather than by how common a condition is.
It prioritises the differential diagnosis
Correct: think horses, not zebras. It also affects the interpretation of test results, because it sets the pretest probability.
It identifies which test is most accurate
Test accuracy is a property of the test, although prevalence does change how its result should be read.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: What distinguishes cumulative incidence from incidence density?
opts: Cumulative incidence uses person-time in the denominator
Person-time is the denominator of incidence density, used because the population changes.
Incidence density counts existing as well as new cases
Both measure new cases; what differs is whether the population is fixed or dynamic.
Cumulative incidence applies only to acute illness
Neither measure is restricted by the acuteness of the condition.
Cumulative incidence uses a group of fixed size
Correct, whereas incidence density measures new cases in a changing population, which is why its denominator is person-time rather than people.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
set2.q: What is the cost of narrowing the population under study?
opts: It always introduces measurement error
Measurement error arises from the process of measuring rather than from how the population was bounded.
It may curtail generalisability
Correct, and the trade is often worth making, as when a study is limited to those in a service region who need the service, but the limit has to be acknowledged.
It makes the rate impossible to calculate
A narrower population still gives a denominator; what suffers is how widely the result applies.
It converts the study into an experiment
Nothing is assigned by narrowing a population, so the design remains observational.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: What does prevalence set when a test result is interpreted?
opts: The pretest probability
Correct, and this is why the same result means different things in different settings: a positive test in a population where the disease is rare is far more often a false positive.
The sensitivity of the test
Sensitivity is a property of the test rather than of the population it is used in.
The specificity of the test
Specificity likewise belongs to the test rather than to how common the disease is.
The reliability of the measurement
Reliability concerns whether repeated measurement gives the same answer, independent of disease frequency.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: What is incidence density useful for?
opts: Populations of fixed size followed together
A group of fixed size is what cumulative incidence handles, counting new cases among a membership that does not change.
Dynamic populations, with people moving in and out
Correct, which is why it is often used in clinical trials, where participants enrol and leave at different times rather than all being present throughout.
Measuring how many people have a condition now
Counting everyone who has a condition at a moment is prevalence rather than any measure of new occurrence.
Comparing mortality between nations
International health comparison is commonly done with the infant mortality rate.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: What principle underlies years of potential life lost?
opts: Deaths should be weighted by the cost of treatment
Cost of treatment is not what the measure weights; age at death is, because dying young costs more productive years.
Death at a younger age loses more productive years
Correct, and the practical use follows: it helps target interventions at the causes that take the most life from a population, not merely the most lives.
All deaths carry equal weight regardless of age
Equal weighting of every death is exactly what this measure departs from, by counting the years each death removed.
Only deaths from preventable causes are counted
The measure weights by age at death rather than restricting to preventable causes.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: In chronic disease, how do incidence and prevalence usually compare?
opts: Incidence is usually higher than prevalence
That pattern belongs to acute illness, where people recover and leave the prevalent pool quickly.
They are usually equal
The relationship depends on how long people remain cases, which differs sharply between chronic and acute conditions.
Incidence is usually lower than prevalence
Correct, because newly diagnosed patients are added to a group that does not shed its existing members, so cases accumulate.
Neither can be measured in chronic disease
Both are measurable; the point is how their relationship differs by the duration of the condition.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: What does the crude mortality rate measure?
opts: Deaths from all causes in a population
Correct, which is why it is called crude: it makes no adjustment for the age structure of the population, and an older population will show a higher figure for that reason alone.
Deaths from one specified cause in a population
That is the cause-specific mortality rate, which narrows the numerator to a single cause.
Deaths within a particular age group
That is the age-specific mortality rate, which narrows both numerator and denominator to one age band.
Deaths among those diagnosed with a disease
That is case fatality, which measures the severity of a disease rather than mortality in a population.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: What does prevalence describe?
opts: The portion who develop a condition over a period
That is incidence, which counts new cases arising in previously healthy people.
The portion of a group with a condition at one time
Correct, and the useful image is a snapshot: it is measured by counting who does and does not have the condition, which is what surveys are good at.
The proportion of those diagnosed who die
That is case fatality, a measure of severity among those diagnosed rather than of how much disease is present.
The number of deaths per unit of population
That describes a mortality rate rather than how much of a condition is present.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: What distinguishes point from period prevalence?
opts: Point prevalence uses the same calendar date for all
The single point is per person and does not need to be the same date across the group.
Period prevalence counts only new cases
Counting only new cases describes incidence; period prevalence counts all cases present.
Point prevalence is a single moment for each person
Correct, and that moment need not be the same calendar date for everyone. Period prevalence counts cases present during a specified stretch of time.
Point prevalence applies only to chronic disease
Neither measure is restricted by the chronicity of the condition.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: Which measure is commonly used to compare health status between nations?
opts: Infant mortality rate
Correct: deaths among children under one year divided by live births in the same period, multiplied by one thousand.
Crude death rate
The crude rate reflects a population's age structure as much as its health, which limits its use for international comparison.
Proportionate mortality
That describes how deaths are distributed among causes rather than how much death there is.
Death-to-case ratio
That compares deaths to new cases of one disease rather than describing a nation's health status.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: Which is a named surveillance strategy?
opts: Reviewing published systematic reviews
Literature synthesis is not one of the surveillance strategies named.
Randomly assigning exposures in the population
Assignment of exposure is experimental and has no place in surveillance.
Pooling data from several published studies
Pooling published studies describes a meta-analysis, which synthesises evidence rather than gathering surveillance data.
Screening high-risk persons or groups
Correct, alongside clinical symptoms and syndromes, mortality data, provider reporting of morbidity and laboratory reporting of positive results.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: A town of 1,000 has 80 cases of a disease in 2015, and 20 previously healthy people develop it between 2016 and 2018. Which figure is the incidence for that period?
opts: Eight per cent
That is the prevalence in 2015, being the 80 cases already present in the 1,000 residents.
Ten per cent
That is the prevalence in 2018, counting all 100 cases present rather than only the new ones.
Eighteen per cent
Adding the 2015 prevalence to the new cases mixes two different measures rather than producing either.
Two per cent
Correct, since 20 new cases in 1,000 people is the new-case count over the period. The 100 cases present in 2018 give a prevalence of ten per cent.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: What does endemic mean?
opts: A concentration of new cases in a given time
A concentration of new cases in a given time is an epidemic, which belongs to distribution by time.
Disease limited by geographic location
Correct, and it belongs to distribution by place, alongside the outbreak lists, travel notices and food safety recalls maintained nationally.
Widespread cases across many regions
Widespread cases describe a pandemic, which may develop rapidly or slowly depending on the disease.
A disease that has been eradicated
Endemic describes a disease confined to an area rather than one that has gone.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: On which three levels is the distribution of disease evaluated?
opts: Agent, host and environment
Those three are what epidemiology sets out to discover as factors affecting health rather than the levels on which distribution is evaluated.
Person, place and time
Correct, and the work of looking for patterns across those three is a large part of what epidemiologists actually do.
Incidence, prevalence and mortality
Those are measures of disease frequency rather than levels of distribution.
Nominal, ordinal and interval
Those are the three types of data that measurement produces.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: Which age range defines the neonatal mortality rate?
opts: 28 to 364 days
That is the postneonatal mortality rate rather than the neonatal one.
Under one year
That is the infant mortality rate, which spans both the neonatal and postneonatal periods.
Under 28 days
Correct, with live births as the denominator. Postneonatal mortality covers 28 to 364 days, and infant mortality covers the whole first year.
Under five years
No measure in this set uses five years; the divisions are 28 days, 28 to 364 days, and the first year.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: What does the 1976 Philadelphia Legionnaires' disease outbreak illustrate?
opts: A slowly developing pandemic
A slow pandemic is illustrated by HIV and AIDS rather than by a localised outbreak after one event.
An endemic disease confined by geography
The outbreak was a concentration of new cases in time rather than a disease permanently limited to an area.
A prevalence survey of a community
Cases were investigated as an outbreak rather than counted in a cross-sectional survey.
An epidemic curve tied to a single gathering
Correct: cases were plotted by date of onset across July and August, following an American Legion convention.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 40

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: What does case fatality measure?
opts: Disease frequency in a population
Frequency is what incidence and prevalence measure; case fatality concerns what happens to those who have the disease.
The distribution of deaths among causes
That is proportionate mortality, which distributes all deaths among their causes rather than measuring severity.
Years of productive life lost to early death
That is years of potential life lost, a separate measure used to target interventions.
Disease severity
Correct, expressed as the proportion of people diagnosed with a disease who die from it, which says nothing about how common the disease is.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: Which is an epidemiologic function of surveillance?
opts: Detecting outbreaks and epidemics

Correct, alongside determining the magnitude of a problem, understanding natural history, documenting geographic spread, testing aetiologic hypotheses, evaluating control strategies and monitoring changes in an agent.
Assigning treatment to individual patients
Treatment of individuals is clinical work rather than a surveillance function.
Publishing systematic reviews of the literature
Evidence synthesis is a separate activity from population surveillance.
Setting the price of preventive services
Setting the price of services is not among the epidemiologic functions of surveillance that are named.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: Where does the potential for error lie in incidence density?
opts: In variation in duration of follow-up
Correct, because person-time treats one person followed ten years as equivalent to ten people followed one year, which may not be true of the risk involved.
In counting existing cases as new ones
Incidence of any kind counts only new cases in previously healthy people.
In the population being of fixed size
A fixed population is what cumulative incidence assumes; incidence density exists for changing ones.
In the multiplier used to express the result
The multiplier scales the figure for legibility rather than introducing error.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: At which levels does disease surveillance operate?
opts: National level only
State and county health departments both take part alongside the national agency.
National, state and county
Correct, and it may be active or passive. Its first contribution is a baseline, without which no rise in cases can be recognised as a rise.
Hospital level only
Hospitals contribute data, but surveillance is organised through national, state and county public health structures.
International level only
The levels named are national, state and county, so surveillance is not run from any single one of them.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: What is an epidemic curve?
opts: The number of cases plotted against location
Location is handled under distribution by place rather than by an epidemic curve.
The proportion of cases that prove fatal
That is case fatality, a measure of how lethal a disease is rather than of how an outbreak spread.
The number of cases plotted against time
Correct, and its shape carries information about the type of exposure, the route of spread and when exposure occurred.
The cumulative attack rate across subgroups
The attack rate is a separate determination from the plot of cases over time.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: Which characteristics of an outbreak are described alongside the epidemic curve?
opts: Case fatality, years of life lost and attack rate
Those are measures of impact rather than the characteristics used to work out how an outbreak spread.
Incidence, prevalence and mortality
Those are measures of disease frequency rather than the characteristics named here.
Type of exposure, route of spread and timing of exposure
Correct, and together they feed the hypotheses about source, type and route of spread that the investigation then tests.
Person, place and time
Those are the three levels on which the distribution of disease is evaluated, a related but separate framework.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: Why may prevalence be lower than incidence in acute illness?
opts: People recover, so few are ill at any one moment
Correct, with the common cold as the example: a great many people are affected over a period while only a small number have it at any given instant.
Acute illnesses are diagnosed less often
The explanation offered is recovery and short duration rather than under-diagnosis.
Acute illnesses have no measurable incidence
Incidence is precisely what is high in acute illness; it is prevalence that stays low because people recover quickly.
Acute illness is not counted in prevalence studies
It is counted; it simply does not persist long enough to accumulate.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
set2.q: What is another name for an incidence study?
opts: A cross-sectional study
Assessing a population for a condition at one moment describes a prevalence study.
A case series
A case series describes a group of cases without a denominator or follow-up.
A meta-analysis
A meta-analysis pools published studies rather than following a population.
A cohort study
Correct, because a population is followed over time to identify whether the condition appears, which is what following a cohort means.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: What distinguishes an epidemic from a pandemic?
opts: An epidemic is widespread; a pandemic is local
The terms run the other way: widespread distribution is what makes an outbreak a pandemic.
An epidemic is limited by geography
Limitation by geographic location defines an endemic disease rather than either kind of outbreak.
A pandemic always develops rapidly
A pandemic may be rapid or slow; HIV and AIDS are given as the slow example.
An epidemic concentrates new cases in time; a pandemic is widespread
Correct, and a pandemic may develop rapidly, as with the influenza outbreak of the early 1900s, or slowly, as with HIV and AIDS.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: What sits in the denominator of the crude death rate?
opts: The total number of deaths from all causes
Deaths in the denominator describes proportionate mortality, which is a fraction of deaths rather than a rate.
The mid-interval population
Correct, and it is multiplied by 1,000 or 100,000 so the result is a legible number rather than a small decimal.
The number of live births in the same interval
Live births form the denominator of the infant, neonatal and maternal mortality rates.
The number of new cases of the disease
New cases in the denominator describes the death-to-case ratio.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
set2.q: What effect does awareness of an epidemic have?
opts: It can make new cases easier to diagnose
Correct, with early COVID-19 as the example. It is also a reason measured frequency can rise partly because clinicians started looking.
It reduces the true incidence of the disease
Awareness changes detection rather than how many people actually fall ill.
It converts an epidemic into a pandemic
What makes an outbreak a pandemic is how widespread it becomes, not how well known it is.
It has no effect on case finding
Easier diagnosis of new cases is precisely the effect described.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

set2.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
set2.q: What does the death-to-case ratio compare?
opts: Deaths from a cause against new cases of it
Correct, both over the same time interval, multiplied by one hundred. It measures how lethal a disease is rather than how much of it there is.
Deaths from a cause against the whole population
A population denominator describes the cause-specific death rate.
Deaths from a cause against all deaths
That describes proportionate mortality, whose denominator is all deaths rather than new cases of the disease.
Deaths against live births
Live birth denominators belong to the infant, neonatal and maternal mortality rates.
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9
